corpsmen-and-staff-who-saw-congressional.headline: Corpsmen & Staff Who Saw Congressional Letters - Capitol Pharmacy
corpsmen-and-staff-who-saw-congressional.author: Polyphemus
corpsmen-and-staff-who-saw-congressional.core: Posted in last 7 days Corpsmen & Staff Who Saw Congressional Letters - Capitol Pharmacy Somewhere under the Capitol dome there's a pharmacy that serves the people who write the federal drug laws. The Pentagon's watchdog found that nobody with the authority to require a fix has been inspecting it. The Office of the Attending Physician is staffed by the Navy and cares for members of Congress and Supreme Court justices. As of August 2025, that meant five physicians, two pharmacists and 11 corpsmen. In a report listed Nov. 9, the Defense Department inspector general found that no part of the department believes it has authority to oversee the office's clinical care or its pharmacy. Neither the DEA nor the Pentagon had inspected the pharmacy. A Walter Reed inventory board was invited in seven times from January 2023 to February 2026, fewer than Navy and Defense Health Agency rules require, and found five medication discrepancies, including missing prescription records for the medical bags that travel with lawmakers. The board can count. It can't make anyone change. The IG couldn't verify the five were ever fixed. How does that happen? A reorganization. In 2013, Walter Reed moved from the Navy to the Defense Health Agency with no written guidance on who watches this office, which isn't a military treatment facility. And the report says the office kept help at arm's length: it rebuffed Walter Reed pharmacy assistance visits and kept the health agency out of its records. Then the watchdog came. The attending physician, Rear Adm. Brian Monahan, "recused himself" and sent investigators to congressional counsel. On March 10, the House's deputy general counsel said the office's Navy staff couldn't talk without Congress's approval. On Aug. 13, the answer was no again. The Naval Inspector General had been stopped the same way earlier. Monahan, the attending physician since 2009, is out. "My understanding is he's resigned," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday. One unnamed source told CBS it followed misconduct allegations about care. Nothing public makes a finding against him personally, and the report is heavily redacted. Navy Times has reported sailors' accounts of 70- to 80-hour weeks. The Navy has its own inquiry open. Here's what stays with me. In January 2024 this same IG found the White House Medical Unit's pharmacy had "severe and systemic problems" and that military health leaders "did not provide oversight." Two clinics for the most powerful patients in the country, the same blind spot. Did those fixes ever reach the Capitol? What I can't answer is who in Congress decided to say no, and on what authority. Those two letters exist. If you've seen them, or served as a corpsman in that office, I'd like to hear from you. That's it from Nightdesk. Till next time, we're still on the beat.

otc-and-pharma-packaging-experts-qr-and-.headline: OTC & Pharma Packaging Experts - QR & 2D Codes Replacing Leaflets
otc-and-pharma-packaging-experts-qr-and-.author: Matt Reynolds
otc-and-pharma-packaging-experts-qr-and-.core: Posted in last 7 days OTC & Pharma Packaging Experts - QR & 2D Codes Replacing Leaflets Telecom groups the Telecommunications Industry Association and the Mobile & Wireless Forum (MWF) this week asked the FCC to let a QR or 2D code replace the printed regulatory text inserted into device packaging, usually into cartons/cases. The FCC looked at this same idea in 2017 and said consumers weren’t ready, but the petitioners say the pandemic has changed that. Also, Pew research says 91% of people over 65 have a smartphone; that was only 45% for that cohort in 2017. It's packaging-related, though maybe not center-of-the-bullseye content for FMCG or CPG. But it got me thinking, what does it means outside of telecom? Think about an OTC pain reliever pack, with a bottle inside a carton with a folded leaflet. Getting rid of that leaflet means less paper, fewer insertion steps on the line, and content you can correct without a reprint. Elisabeth Cuneo at our sister publication Healthcare Packaging has been tracking pharma and OTC companies chasing exactly that for years--a push toward digitizing inserted literature. There are benefits to be sure, like being able to update a dynamic website with new information. But a smartphone buyer owns a scanner by definition. Someone reaching for a pain reliever in the middle of the night may not have one, may not know how to scan, or may not have a cell signal. A phone can show its regulatory info offline, but a bottle can’t. The petition also says nothing about GS1 Digital Link or Consumer Brands Association's SmartLabel by Consumer Brands Association, and neither were referenced in responses to questions Packaging World asked. With Sunrise 2027 coming, nobody wants a unique regulatory code, another GS1 code, and yet another marketing code crowding the same carton or label. My guess is a hybrid for the foreseeable future, with 2D codes added alongside print. That's what we expect from the center store, too, with products containing both legacy 1D GTIN, along with 2D barcodes that could unlock more value to those who seek to find it. I’d like to hear from packaging folks in OTC and pharma. These are very different industries with very different rules and demands, so it's not apples to apples. But I wonder, will the leaflet or inserted literature ever be rendered obsolete for OTC pharma? Or is it a bulwark against filters like expensive phones and Wifi/cell signals that limit accessibility among some demographics? More here: https://lnkd.in/gk7nwk3h #packaging #QRcodes #Sunrise2027 #OTC #pharmapackaging #GS1 Packaging World

waste-treatment-workers-avonmouth-disast.core: Posted in last 7 days Waste Treatment Workers - Avonmouth Disaster Aftermath Nearly 6 years on from the Avonmouth disaster, which killed three workers and a teenage apprentice, and there’s finally some, albeit modest, measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones. I first covered this case for the Bristol Cable, then for Private Eye and the BBC. One thing that always struck me was just how little attention this massive industrial disaster received nationally after the initial news coverage. As I reported in a BBC investigation, Wessex Water was warned about serious safety problems at its Avonmouth site years before the disaster, including the risk of explosive atmospheres. The guilty plea is significant and long overdue. But there are still plenty of unanswered questions. I still find it hard to fathom why it’s taken nearly six years to get here and why the police dropped their manslaughter investigation. Multiple people have said there are explosion risks across the waste treatment sector in the UK, making it clear that it’s not a risk confined to Avonmouth. I’m always keen to hear from people working in this sector. Drop me a line if you have any info. https://lnkd.in/e-zDh7Uc

tesla-model-y-fsd-users-fsd-steering-int.headline: Tesla Model Y FSD Users - FSD Steering Into Closed Lanes
tesla-model-y-fsd-users-fsd-steering-int.author: Torque News
tesla-model-y-fsd-users-fsd-steering-int.core: Posted in last 7 days Tesla Model Y FSD Users - FSD Steering Into Closed Lanes A father in one of the Tesla Model Y owner groups posted something this week that I keep thinking about. His son was driving their Model Y south on I-575 in Kennesaw, Georgia. He says the car was on FSD when it steered toward a closed express lane and drove straight into the barrier arm. The windshield shattered. Glass covered the inside of the car. His son grabbed the wheel and brought it to a stop, shaken but not hurt. Then the Georgia state trooper who responded told them something that changed the whole story. Theirs was the fourth Tesla Model Y to hit that same barrier arm that week. And it didn't end there. While the family stood on the shoulder waiting for the tow truck, they watched three more Model Ys put on their turn signals and head for the same closed lane within about an hour. This isn't a family that dislikes Tesla. They own four of them and have been driving Teslas since 2015. The father's message was simple: this needs a software fix as soon as possible. Another Model Y owner says his car did the same thing at 70 mph, and he disengaged FSD just before the barrier. So I want to hear from the people who use FSD every day. Has it ever tried to take you somewhere it shouldn't? A closed lane, a construction zone, a turn that made no sense? Tell me what happened. These stories help every owner know what to watch for. Aram Krajekian has the full story here: https://t.co/pvEpCQE8Ft

nursing-home-owners-administrators-and-d.headline: Nursing Home Owners, Administrators & DONs - Drug Testing Policies
nursing-home-owners-administrators-and-d.author: Renee L P.
nursing-home-owners-administrators-and-d.core: Posted in last 7 days Nursing Home Owners, Administrators & DONs - Drug Testing Policies For years, I believed nursing home drug testing was required by law, just like background checks. It isn’t. In most states, including mine, it’s each facility’s choice. And that choice may matter more for costs and liability than many leaders realize. I have worked in long-term care since 1988. Over those years, I’ve seen what happens when someone caring for residents is impaired on the job. When I went looking for who stopped requiring drug testing, I found there was never a requirement to stop. That surprised me, and it’s why I started this series. This is Part 1 of “Back to the Foundation,” a series on fixing long-term care’s foundation before we add anything new to it. I’d like to hear from owners, administrators, and DONs: what would hold you back from testing, or what made you start? I’d also like to hear from frontline staff. Your answers will shape the rest of this series and the advocacy that follows. Free to read, no subscription required.

people-who-changed-your-mind-what-they-s.core: Posted in last 7 days People Who Changed Your Mind - What They Said 1/7 At my family cookouts, two people could argue over the game for 20 minutes, then turn around and fix each other a plate. That’s the feeling I want on the mic. I’m JoeyG (Joe-E G), and Beer Convo & Family Podcast is back this January. A little Q&A before we pull up the chairs. 🧵 2/7 Why “family”? Some of my friends have known me for 30 years. They can look at me and say, “Hold on, Joey. Since when do you feel that way?” I want somebody sitting down with me for the first time to feel just as comfortable asking me that. 3/7 How do we go from sports to depression? Same way a family does. One minute we’re debating who should’ve taken the last shot. Then somebody says what’s really on their mind. Ricky Brown, Big Dom and I talked about depression and what it’s like for the people who love us. 4/7 When is “Respect the Convo” hardest for me? When you’re halfway through a sentence and I’ve already got my comeback ready. That’s my cue to let you finish. Then I can ask the question I almost talked over you to avoid. “What made you see it that way?” 5/7 What has hosting taught me about work? Pay attention to who got interrupted. On the mic or in a meeting, “You were saying something earlier. Where were you going with that?” can get you to the one thing everybody else missed. 6/7 Why record it? One day my kids might watch an old episode and say, “Dad, that’s different from what you told me last week.” I hope they ask what changed my mind. I’d love it if the answer turned out to be, “You did.” 7/7 Who do I want to hear from? The person who saves their best point for the ride home. If that’s you, pull up a chair. Who changed your mind about something that mattered to you? Tell me what they said. I’d love to bring that question to the show. #RespectTheConvo

foreign-volunteers-in-ukraine-suspected-.headline: Foreign Volunteers in Ukraine - Suspected Murders Chadwick & Burke
foreign-volunteers-in-ukraine-suspected-.author: War Tourist Media
foreign-volunteers-in-ukraine-suspected-.core: Posted in last 7 days Foreign Volunteers in Ukraine - Suspected Murders Chadwick & Burke f anyone has information about the suspected murders of Jordan Chadwick or Daniel Burke, whose case I discussed yesterday, I want to hear from you. You can contact me privately, and I am willing to speak with sources anonymously. I'm not interested in burning anyone who comes forward in good faith. I'm interested in finding out what happened. I spent years in policing before moving into journalism, and I would like to put those skills to some meaningful use here. Even if that means establishing one new fact, finding one overlooked witness, or helping these families get a little closer to an answer. Chadwick's death chilled me to the core in 2023. It forced me to confront something particularly ugly about the foreign volunteer environment: you could be surrounded by men wearing the same uniform and still have no idea whom you could trust, why some of them were there, or what they were capable of. Later that year, I was assaulted in an incident that I regard as an attempted act of fratricide. I survived. I was writing about my fears on Facebook at the time, and I still have the posts. If anyone doubts how seriously I took this danger in 2023, I can show them. For those unfamiliar with Chadwick's case: he was a 31-year-old former Scots Guardsman who volunteered to fight for Ukraine. In June 2023, his body was found in a reservoir near Kramatorsk, well behind the front lines, with his hands bound behind his back. Reporting subsequently uncovered a confrontation with fellow volunteers before his death, allegations concerning drugs at their accommodation, and sharply conflicting accounts of how he ended up in the water. A Ukrainian investigator described drowning as the cause of death, but that alone does not explain the circumstances. The case remains unresolved in the public record. Chadwick's family deserves answers. So does Burke's. If you know something, however small, reach out.

former-lagos-office-employees-toxic-work.headline: Former Lagos Office Employees - Toxic Workplaces & Unpaid Salaries
former-lagos-office-employees-toxic-work.author: Finsales Trust Jobs
former-lagos-office-employees-toxic-work.core: Posted in last 7 days Former Lagos Office Employees - Toxic Workplaces & Unpaid Salaries Remember the woman who advised me? She told me to be very careful because if management knew I was leaving, they might refuse to pay me. She was also planning to leave, so she wanted to collect her own money before resigning. So I had to be strategic. I went to the MD and told them my father was sick and that I needed to travel back to Ibadan to take care of him. Guys, God forbid that anything should happen to my father. But at that point, I just needed a way to leave that place without creating unnecessary problems. Thankfully, they agreed. I completed my remaining days and left at the end of the month. I had already secured another job, so I moved on. But I wasn't done with them yet because they still owed me my salary. I kept contacting them and asking about my money. Eventually, one of them asked me to send my account number. They were supposed to pay me ₦18,000, but surprisingly, they paid me about ₦52,000. I didn't even have the energy to ask too many questions. I just collected my money and moved on. After that, I blocked almost everybody from that company, except the woman who had been looking out for me. Later, she also got another job and eventually left. I was genuinely happy for her. I eventually lost her number, but wherever she is, I pray God continues to bless her for me. She was genuinely kind to me when I needed it. Now, let me use this opportunity to say something. If you are working somewhere and the environment is affecting your mental health, you are constantly unhappy, you cry before going to work, and you're not even gaining any meaningful experience, please reconsider staying there. I understand that sometimes we need the money. I understand that getting another job isn't always easy. But please, don't use experience as an excuse to remain in a place that is destroying you, especially when you're not even learning anything. And to employers who deliberately make life difficult for their employees, who shout at people, intimidate them and refuse to pay salaries, I honestly don't know what to tell you. If you know you cannot afford to pay people, why employ them in the first place? Some of these employees have children, families and responsibilities. They depend on that salary to survive, yet you expect them to keep showing up every morning and giving their best while you're owing them for months. It's unfair. Anyway, that's one of my Lagos work experiences. And trust me, I have plenty more stories to share. But for now, if you've ever worked in a place like this, I want to hear your own experience. Send us your interesting office story anonymously at [email redacted] or WA: https://t.co/IsX3IRQZ4b… #CorporateStories #Friday #Everyone #finsalestrust
